title: Use a static method reference `Integer::parseInt` to convert a list of string numbers to integers.
shortTitle: Use a static method reference Integer::parseInt to convert a list of string numbers to integers

s1_definition.profdef: A static method reference `Type::staticMethod` refers to a static method as a functional value. `Integer::parseInt` serves as a `Function<String, Integer>` (or `ToIntFunction`), parsing each string into an int when used in `map` or `mapToInt`.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya receives amounts written as text and needs them as real numbers to add up. Instead of writing "take the text and parse it", she points at the built-in parse tool and runs each text through it.
s1_definition.oneliner: `Integer::parseInt` is a static method reference that turns each numeric string into an int in a stream.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A static method reference `Type::staticMethod` refers to a static method as a functional value. `Integer::parseInt` serves as a `Function<String, Integer>` (or `ToIntFunction`), parsing each string into an int when used in `map` or `mapToInt`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya receives amounts written as text and needs them as real numbers to add up. Instead of writing "take the text and parse it", she points at the built-in parse tool and runs each text through it.

**One line to remember:** `Integer::parseInt` is a static method reference that turns each numeric string into an int in a stream.

sections.s2_technical:
`Integer::parseInt` references the static method `parseInt(String)` and matches any functional interface whose single method takes a String and returns an int-compatible value. In `strings.stream().map(Integer::parseInt)` it produces a `Stream<Integer>`, while `strings.stream().mapToInt(Integer::parseInt)` produces a primitive `IntStream` for efficient numeric aggregation.

This is cleaner than `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)` and expresses intent directly. For the primitive route you can then call `sum()`, `average()`, and so on without boxing. Static references are distinguished from instance references because no receiver object is involved — the argument is passed straight to the static method.

The senior nuance is error handling: `parseInt` throws `NumberFormatException` on malformed input, and because a method reference has no room for a try-catch, a single bad value aborts the whole stream. In production I either pre-validate, or wrap parsing in a helper that returns an Optional and filter out the empties, so one dirty record does not fail the batch. Choosing a static reference assumes the inputs are already clean or that failing fast is acceptable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A feed at the National Bank of India delivers transaction counts as text, and a report must convert them to integers and total them.

This is exactly what a static method reference does — mapping each string through Integer parseInt yields the numeric values ready to sum.

The code defines a `ParseService.toInts` and `sum` method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the strings "10", "25", "7".

Step 1: map with Integer::parseInt parses each string into an Integer, giving 10, 25, 7.

Step 2: toList collects them into a list of integers.

Step 3: In the sum method, mapToInt parses each string straight into a primitive int.

Step 4: sum totals the primitive ints to 42.

```
INFO: parsed: [10, 25, 7]
INFO: sum   : 42
```

```
  │  + sum(List): int              │ mapToInt(parseInt).sum()
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. stream().mapToInt(Integer::parseInt)
  2. sum()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A static method reference treats a static method as a functional value. Integer colon colon parseInt references the static parseInt method and matches a functional interface taking a String and returning an int, so mapping a stream of numeric strings through it parses each one. If I use map I get a stream of Integer objects, and if I use mapToInt I get a primitive IntStream that I can sum or average without any boxing.

At the National Bank of India I used this to turn a text feed of transaction counts into numbers and total them, and the static reference reads more cleanly than the lambda s to Integer parseInt of s. The distinguishing feature from an instance reference is that there is no receiver object — the argument is passed straight into the static method.

The senior point I stress is error handling. parseInt throws a NumberFormatException on malformed input, and because a method reference has no room for a try-catch, a single bad value aborts the entire stream. So in production I either pre-validate the inputs or wrap the parse in a helper that returns an Optional and filter out the failures, which keeps one dirty record from failing the whole batch. A bare static reference is the right choice only when the inputs are already clean or when failing fast is genuinely acceptable.
